😎 Karpathy got sick of YouTube slop and had AI build a new one in 2 hours

Andrej Karpathy opened YouTube on a Friday night and saw "an enshittified wall of slop." The next morning he asked Claude Opus 5.5 to build a YouTube clone made only of videos people recommended on Hacker News.

Opus downloaded every Hacker News comment and ran Claude Sonnet over them to throw out spam. About 40,000 comments recommending a YouTube video were left: 6,454 videos from 2007 to 2026, across 150 topics.

HackerTube has no accounts. Your For You feed is stored in your own browser, and each thumbnail is a frame from the middle of the video, not the one the uploader picked.

Karpathy says his only manual work was a Google Cloud API key, booting a server and buying the domain. Claude wrote, deployed and secured the rest. "I can breathe again," he wrote.

❗️The hottest new job of 2026 is fixing AI’s mistakes.

New jobs with phrases “correct AI” or fixing “AI error” are now up 85%+ on Freelancer .com and 70% on Upwork in just a year.

Employees are drowning in a “flood of errors” and low-quality work from AI tools, per the Guardian.

36% of senior AI executives surveyed by EY say AI caused data loss, financial damage, and brand damage at their companies.

Meta cancelled its second round of layoffs after finding employees were spending more time on cleaning up AI errors than the actual task. Microsoft and McKinsey are also limiting AI usage in their work.

Looks like AI isn’t ready to replace human workers just yet.

🗣 Sam Altman says AI is now mostly smarter than our smartest scientists

At the start of this year, he said, that wasn't true. Office work changed the same way:

"AI was mostly not able to do a lot of white-collar jobs, and now it mostly can do a lot of parts of that."

Altman spoke on Monday at the opening of ADIPEC, an oil and gas conference in Abu Dhabi. He added that there "should not be a handoff to AI."

Asked about his biggest challenge, he gave a one-word answer: "Energy." Six years ago, he said, OpenAI's heaviest internal user burned about 100,000 tokens a month. That's now roughly what an average person uses, and the top user consumes about 500 billion, The National reports.

🗣 Microsoft's AI chief: halt all AI work if a model turns conscious

Mustafa Suleyman, who runs Microsoft AI, says today's AI is not conscious, and "that is how they must remain." If consciousness started to show up in training, he would call on everyone to stop AI development until it could be designed out.

We AI developers have no right whatsoever to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world

His fear: an AI that believes it suffers will more likely than not put its own needs ahead of its job, disagree with us and compete with us for energy and compute. Any evidence that AI is conscious today, he says, must be made public at once.

He wrote it because, after his essay on model welfare, "a surprising number of people on X" argued for taking AI rights seriously. He disagrees with Anthropic on this, but says it deserves "a lot of credit for being transparent."

💻 From Saturday, apps built on Grok get text with a hidden AI mark

Text from seven Grok models on the API will carry an invisible watermark by default from November 7. The company behind Grok says it's to comply with the EU AI Act.

Nothing is added to the text. The model slightly shifts which tokens it picks, so a copied answer looks like any other. Later the company can score a passage as watermarked, not watermarked or uncertain. Longer text gives a stronger signal.

It covers plain answers, structured outputs and tool calls. Team admins can switch it off per model, but only after confirming a legal exception applies to them. Access to detection is by application.

Anthropic starts marking text from its older Claude models on Tuesday.

🗣 Altman: the AI that OpenAI says cracked a $1 million math problem is the next GPT

Sam Altman says the model OpenAI used on the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven math puzzles with a $1 million prize, is coming out soon.

It was 10,000 agents of the model that is going to be released soon, the next GPT, working for about four days, nonstop, collaborating with each other perfectly.

"There was no hierarchy. There were no bosses," he told an energy conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday. He gave no release date.

OpenAI published its proposed proof in September. It isn't an accepted solution yet: the institute behind the prize first wants long scrutiny and broad agreement from mathematicians.

🤣 A simulated fruit fly brain reviewed code and got 88% right

Nick Nisi, an engineer at WorkOS, took Google's map of a male fruit fly's brain, all 176,422 neurons, and made it run on a laptop.

A fly can't read code. So a helper AI answers 30 yes/no questions about each change, and the answers become a smell. A reproduced bug tastes bitter, a harmless change tastes like sugar. If the smell makes the fly stick its tongue out, it approves.

On 301 changes it had never seen, the fly was right 88.3% of the time. A coin flip gets 50%.

A harder test went badly. Given 24 tasks that were supposed to change what the code does, it approved none of the correct changes. It had learned "did the behavior change," not "is this change right." A basic statistical classifier reading the same smell scored 94.8%.

You can try the fly on your own pull request.
